summary:
Argus (argus102.space) is a free web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change. NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, but its data are tens of thousands of separate exposures built for specialists. Type any position or star name and, in about 20 seconds, Argus reads only the pixels it needs from NASA's open archive, cleans and aligns every exposure, and plays the visits like a flipbook. Blink, subtract or stack them, switch between six detectors, and read the brightness and spectrum of any source.

Argus does not stop at showing images. An automatic finder measures every source on every visit, fits its motion, tests its brightness and colour, and checks it against ESA's Gaia catalogue, so unexplained objects stand out. It recovers the motions of Barnard's Star and the brown dwarf ε Indi B in agreement with Gaia, and flags the coldest known brown dwarf, WISE 0855, as a red moving object Gaia cannot see. A Planet X overlay shows how a distant planet would reveal itself, honestly stated as a teaching tool.

Argus turns a new NASA survey into something students, citizen scientists and the curious can explore, share and learn from.
details:
What Argus does


Argus (argus102.space) makes NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey something anyone can explore. Type a position or a star's name, and Argus builds an aligned flipbook of every SPHEREx visit to that patch of sky. Things that move jump between frames, and things that change brightness pulse. Five precomputed targets open instantly. Any other spot is built live in about 15–25 seconds.

  • Blink, difference and stack. Flip between visits. Subtract a reference visit (cyan is brighter now, magenta brighter before, so a moving star becomes a magenta-to-cyan pair). Or add every visit for the deepest image.
  • Six detectors (0.75–5 µm). Cold objects appear only at long wavelengths: the brown dwarf WISE 0855 is invisible below about 3.5 µm and clear in detector D6.
  • Automatic candidate finder. Argus measures every source on every visit. It fits its motion, tests its brightness for variability and its colour for brown-dwarf-like redness, and matches it to ESA's Gaia catalogue. It labels each source moving, variable, very red, not in Gaia or needs follow-up, with markers on the image and the numbers in a panel.
  • Checked against Gaia.Gaia's predicted positions and motion arrows can be overlaid, and every preset target is measured against them. All five agree to within half a pixel.
  • Planet X overlay. It shows how far a distant planet would appear to jump between visits as Earth orbits the Sun (about 14′ at 500 AU). It is presented honestly: such a planet is far too faint for one SPHEREx visit, so the overlay teaches the method rather than claiming a detection.
  • Light curve and spectrum. These are shown for the source at the centre. Each exposure sees a different wavelength, so one visit yields a low-resolution spectrum.
  • Sharing. Every view has its own link. The viewer can be embedded in any website, and you can download a PDF technical report or a GIF of the blink.

How it works

  1. The server asks NASA/IPAC IRSA's image search which SPHEREx exposures cover the position and groups them into visits.
  2. Instead of downloading 65 MB files, it reads only the needed byte ranges from the open archive on Amazon S3, in three parallel rounds. This cut one benchmark from 126 s to 28 s.
  3. Each exposure has the zodiacal-light model subtracted and bad pixels masked. It is then reprojected onto one north-up grid, and each visit is stacked with inverse-variance weights.
  4. Frames reach the browser as compressed 16-bit floats. The browser decodes them in a worker and runs the candidate finder in a few milliseconds.

Results

  • Barnard's Star: the finder, run without being told the targets, measures 11.0 ± 0.7″/yr, against 10.4 from Gaia.
  • ε Indi B: 4.8 ± 0.6″/yr, against 4.7.
  • WISE 0855: flagged as a red moving object Gaia cannot see. Its speed is underestimated because a nearby star blends with it, which we report openly.
  • False positives: no false movers across five 8′ test fields.

Every equation, validation table and limitation is published in a paper-style page at argus102.space/about.

Benefits and intended impact


SPHEREx's public data are tens of thousands of separate exposures in an archive built for scientists. Argus removes that barrier: no account, no code and no download, and it works on phones. It is meant for:

  • Students and teachers: see proper motion, parallax and infrared colour with real NASA data.
  • Citizen scientists: the same blink method that found Pluto, and that volunteers use today in Backyard Worlds, now for SPHEREx, with candidates flagged automatically.
  • Researchers: a quick look at any field and its variability before downloading anything.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, reproject, s3fs/fsspec, httpx, server-sent events, SQLite
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Web Workers, Canvas 2D, Aladin Lite (sky map), jsPDF and gifenc (exports), driver.js (guided tour)
  • Data: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 (NASA/IPAC IRSA, via the SIA2 image search and its open S3 copy); Gaia DR3 (ESA archive)
  • Infrastructure: Docker, Railway, a persistent volume for the cache and counters, Umami analytics (no cookies)
  • Testing: pytest and Vitest, including synthetic star fields that check the finder recovers known motions and variability

What makes it creative


  • It turns a spectral survey into a time machine: one tool shows motion, brightness change and colour together.
  • The finder is built for SPHEREx's quirks:
  • It searches a long-wavelength-only image so the coldest brown dwarfs are not missed.
  • A source counts as variable only when two detectors agree, because SPHEREx's filter shows each source at a different wavelength on each visit.
  • It cancels the tiny alignment shifts shared by the whole field before measuring motion.
  • The Planet X overlay uses the exact Earth-orbit geometry, so users learn why a search looks for a jump rather than a dot.

Factors we considered


  • Scientific honesty: every motion is checked against Gaia, limits are stated plainly (saturated stars, blended sources, too few visits for parallax), and Planet X is not oversold.
  • Accessibility: plain-language labels, a first-visit welcome and a 19-step guided tour, keyboard shortcuts, colour pairs with legends, and reduced-motion support.
  • Speed and cost: partial reads, caching and precomputed presets keep the site fast and cheap to run, with limits that protect NASA's archive.
  • Privacy: no accounts, no cookies, and anonymous counters only.
  • Openness: the code is public at github.com/102-bands/argus, the method is published, and the data are credited with their DOIs.
